newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina seen heading for big soybean harvest.
newsitem.headline: Argentina seen heading for big soybean harvest.

text.p: Argentina's mainly damp summer is proving to be healthy weather for the 1996/97 soybean crop, which is heading to beat last season's output by over one million tonnes, traders and analysts said Tuesday.
But, while the state of most of the beans is good, there remain two recalcitrant pockets of dryness in the Rafael area in the northwest of Santa Fe province, and in Cordoba.

"It's very dry in Rafaela and in parts of Cordoba. I would say Rafaela makes up probably five percent of the total soybean area, and Cordoba probably a little more," a trader told Reuters, "All in all I'd say 10-12 percent of the soybean area is dry and the rest is good. Better than normal."

He said that he was working with a forecast of output of 13.5 million tonnes, below the Agriculture Secretariat's forecast of 13.7 million tonnes but up from last year's harvest of 12.4 million tonnes.

"Overall the single crop beans are in very good shape," he said, "Some of the double crop has suffered, especially in the areas I mentioned. In some areas it is so bad that there are lots which won't be harvested."
The beans are now mainly moving into pod filling, with the double crop third of the crop a little more advanced.
The soy has benefitted from a regular pattern of rain in most crop lands this season. But the same rain has hit the sunflower crop, allowing esclerotinia fungus to flourish in some areas.
Armando Casalins of the Grain Elevators Association agreed that the soybean crop was coming along nicely, and said he thought output would be 13.6-13.7 million tonnes.
But he expressed concern about the effects of the insect-borne Rio Cuarto virus which has hit the maize crop,
"We think the damage could run to 500,000 tonnes of lost output," he said.
This would reduce the association's previous estimate of maize production, which was at 14.2-14.3 million tonnes before the Rio Cuarto problem hit.
But Casalins stressed that the patchy nature of the Rio Cuarto outbreak made it hard to form an accurate idea of how much production would be lost.
The government recently forecast maize output of 14.6 million tonnes, up from 10.5 million tonnes last season. The first maize harvesting is just beginning.
Casalins was fairly cheerful about the prospects for the sunflower crop, despite the wet weather and esclerotinia. He said he thought output would total around 5.4 million tonnes.
The trader said, "I've heard mixed comments about the sunflower. I think yields will be more or less in line with last year and I'm sticking to 5.5 million tonnes."
But he added that the area wost hit by esclerotinia has been southeast Buenos Aires, where many farmers opted for soybeans instead of sunflowers and so sidestepped the problem.
Farmers produced 5.4 million tonnes of sunflower seed in 1995/96, and the government is forecasting a slightly larger crop this season, at 5.6 million tonnes.
Sunflower harvesting is now starting in western Buenos Aires, but the crop still has a chance to suffer if it is hit by heavy rains or wind.
